R01 The snow began before the caravan reached the pass, light at first and then thick enough to hide the lead wagon.

R02 Tamsin walked beside the mules with a scarf over her mouth and her hands buried deep in the sleeves of her coat.

R03 The guide had promised shelter at the old toll house, but nobody in the line had seen it for nearly an hour.

R04 Behind her, the cook was singing a marching song to keep the children moving, off key and very loud.

R05 The road narrowed until the wheels ran a hand's width from the drop, and the drivers stopped talking at all.

R06 At the first switchback a lantern swung on a post, though no one had lit it and no one stood beside it.

R07 Tamsin touched the glass. It was warm, and the flame inside burned without a wick, a small blue knot of light.

R08 She said nothing about it to the others. The guide looked at the lantern, then at her, and walked on faster.

R09 A second lantern hung at the next bend, and a third beyond that, each one placed exactly where the road turned.

R10 Whoever had set them knew the pass better than the guide did, and seemed to want the caravan to get through.

R11 By dusk the wind had dropped, and the snow fell straight down in large soft flakes that made no sound at all.

R12 The toll house appeared all at once, a squat stone building with a roof bowed under a mound of white.

R13 Its door was open. A fire burned in the hearth, and a kettle hung over it, already beginning to steam.

R14 There were forty cups set out on the long table, which was exactly the number of travellers in the caravan.

R15 The cook counted them twice and then sat down heavily on the bench, his song forgotten for the first time.

R16 The children did not care who had laid the table. They crowded around the fire and held their hands to it.

R17 Tamsin went back outside to see to the mules and found fresh hay in the stalls and water in every trough.

R18 In the last stall a man sat on an upturned bucket, mending a harness by the light of one more blue lantern.

R19 He wore a toll keeper's coat, faded nearly grey, with brass buttons that had not been polished in years.

R20 "You are late," he said, without looking up. "The pass closes at sundown. I kept it open for you."

R21 Tamsin asked how he had known they were coming. He shrugged and pulled the waxed thread tight with his teeth.

R22 "Somebody always comes," he said. "Somebody always thinks the snow will wait for them. It never does."

R23 He asked for the toll. She reached for her purse, but he shook his head and pointed at her scarf instead.

R24 It was an old scarf, knitted by her grandmother, blue and white in a pattern of small interlocking keys.

R25 She gave it to him. He folded it carefully and laid it on a shelf among a hundred other folded scarves.

R26 Every one of them was patterned with keys, and every pattern was a little different from all the others.

R27 "Your grandmother paid the same toll," he said. "And her mother before her. It is a family road, this one."

R28 Tamsin did not remember her grandmother ever crossing the mountains. She said so, and the keeper laughed.

R29 "Nobody remembers the pass," he said. "That is part of the toll as well. You will forget me by the spring."

R30 She went back into the toll house. The kettle had boiled, and the cook was pouring tea into the forty cups.

R31 The guide sat apart from the others, staring into the fire with the look of a man doing difficult sums.

R32 When Tamsin sat beside him he said quietly that he had made this crossing nine times and never seen the house.

R33 She told him about the keeper and the scarves. He listened without interrupting and then asked to see the stall.

R34 They went out together. The stall was empty, the bucket stood upright, and the shelf held no scarves at all.

R35 Only one blue lantern remained, hanging over the door, and it was already going out as they watched it.

R36 In the morning the snow had stopped, the sky was hard and clear, and the road down the far side was open.

R37 The caravan left the toll house as they had found it, with the door open and a fire banked in the hearth.

R38 Tamsin walked at the back of the line, her neck cold without the scarf, trying to fix the keeper's face.

R39 By the time they reached the valley she could recall his coat and his buttons, but not his voice or his eyes.

R40 By spring she remembered only that her scarf was gone, and that she had not minded giving it away.
